LESSON 1
Cherry Blossoms: Color and Emphasis
Instructional Content · Week 1: Learn & Look
📖 ESSENTIAL QUESTION
When you look at a picture, why does your eye stop on one spot first? And how do artists use color to give that spot its power?
In a landscape full of trees, hills, and sky, your eye does not wander forever. It lands somewhere first. Artists plan that on purpose. This week you will learn how Japanese printmakers used color and a focal point (also called emphasis) to lead your eye exactly where they wanted it to go.
🎯 BY THE END OF THIS LESSON YOU WILL BE ABLE TO…
1
I will be able to tell warm colors from cool colors and say what mood each one gives.
2
I will be able to find the focal point (emphasis) in a landscape and explain how the artist made it stand out.
3
I will be able to plan a cherry-blossom landscape with one clear focal point of my own.
👀 PART 1 · LOOK FIRST

Before we name anything, let's look.

This is a color woodblock print made in Japan during the Edo period (about 1603 to 1868 A.D.) by an artist named Utagawa Hiroshige. It shows a hillside in spring where cherry trees are blooming. Every spring in Japan, people gather under the blossoming trees to picnic and enjoy them. This tradition has a name, hanami, which means "flower viewing." Spend a full minute looking before you read on.

🧠 SEE · NOTICE · WONDER

👀 What do you SEE? A hillside covered in clouds of soft pink cherry blossoms. Tiny people walk among the trees and sit together on the grass. A band of deep blue sky stretches across the top, and a pale mountain sits far away on the left.

🔍 What do you NOTICE? The pink blossoms are the brightest, warmest thing in the whole picture. The hill, the sky, and the distant mountain are all cool blues and greens. Your eye keeps landing on the pink.

💭 What do you WONDER? Why does the pink feel so warm and alive against all that blue and green? By the end of this lesson you will be able to answer that, using color and emphasis.

📚 PART 2 · NAME WHAT YOU SEE

Two ideas: Color and Emphasis

Last time you met all seven Elements of Art. This week we zoom in on one element, color, and one principle, emphasis. Watch for both inside Hiroshige's print.

Warm colors and cool colors

🔥
WARM COLORS — reds, oranges, yellows, and pinks. They remind us of fire and sunlight, so they feel close and lively. In the print: the pink blossoms are warm.
❄️
COOL COLORS — blues, greens, and purples. They remind us of water, sky, and shade, so they feel calm and far away. In the print: the hill, the sky, and the distant mountain are cool.
A quick look at WARM & COOL COLORS — the pink blossoms feel warm and close, while the blue sky and green hillside feel cool and calm; artists balance the two on purpose.

Emphasis: the focal point

🎯
EMPHASIS — the part of an artwork that stands out the most and grabs your eye first. The spot that wins your attention is called the focal point (or center of interest).

Artists create emphasis on purpose. A few of their tricks:

• Contrast of color: one warm spot in a cool picture (the pink blossoms against the blue and green).
• Brightness: the brightest area pulls the eye.
• Difference: the one thing that is not like its neighbors stands out.
• Placement: putting it where the eye naturally travels.

In the print, the pink blossoms are the focal point. They are warm in a cool scene and they are the brightest color, so your eye goes to them again and again. The calm blue sky and distant mountain do not compete; they let the blossoms win.

✂️ QUICK CHECK · COLOR & EMPHASIS
Use what you just read about Hiroshige's print. Tap your answer.
The pink of the cherry blossoms is which kind of color?
Which part of the print is the focal point, the spot your eye lands on first?
What mainly makes the blossoms stand out so strongly?
🔎 PART 3 · WATCH IT WORK

How an artist reads a picture

Artists look in a careful order: first they describe, then they analyze, then they interpret, and only then do they judge. Watch how it works on Hiroshige's cherry-blossom print.

DESCRIBE — what is there? A green hillside full of blooming pink cherry trees, small people walking and picnicking, a village at the lower left, a deep blue sky, and a pale mountain far away.
ANALYZE — how is it built? Warm pink color sits against cool blue and green, so the blossoms become the focal point (emphasis). Near trees look big and the far mountain looks tiny, which creates deep space.
INTERPRET — what might it mean? Spring is a happy, gentle season. The warm blossoms feel alive and welcoming, and the calm cool background makes the day feel peaceful.
JUDGE — does it succeed? Most viewers say yes. The single warm focal point makes the picture easy to enjoy, and you feel the joy of a spring flower-viewing day.
💡 YOUR TURN IS COMING

This week you will make a Cherry Blossom Landscape of your own: a white moon, a cool blue sky, and a dark branch covered in warm pink blossoms. The blossoms and moon will be your focal point, made to stand out exactly the way Hiroshige made his blossoms stand out.

⚠️ WORTH KNOWING · AI & ART
An AI image generator can produce a pretty cherry-blossom scene from a few words. It cannot make the choices that are yours to make: deciding where you want the eye to land (emphasis) and mixing the colors by your own hand. Those decisions are what turn a picture into your artwork.
📚 VOCABULARY
Color
What we see when light reflects off a surface.
Warm colors
Reds, oranges, yellows, pinks; feel close and lively.
Cool colors
Blues, greens, purples; feel calm and far away.
Emphasis
The part that stands out most and grabs the eye first.
Focal point
The spot that wins your attention; the center of interest.
Contrast
A strong difference (warm vs. cool, light vs. dark).
Hanami
The Japanese spring tradition of cherry-blossom viewing.
Woodblock print
A picture carved into wood, inked, and pressed onto paper.

💪 THE BIG IDEA

Color carries mood (warm feels close and lively, cool feels calm and far), and emphasis decides where the eye lands first. Put a warm focal point in a cool scene, like Hiroshige's pink blossoms, and you control what the viewer notices. That is a choice every artist gets to make.
